body: IPO May 2002 at $15. Splits 2:1 (2004), 7:1 (2015), 10:1 (Nov 17 2025) = 140x, so IPO ~$0.11 on today's basis. Crash 1 (Qwikster): July 2011 peak ~$305 pre-2015-split (~$4.35 today) -> Sept 2012 low ~$53 (~$0.76), about -80%; AP: -75% from mid-July to Dec 2011, $12bn wiped, ~800k-2m subs lost after a ~60% price hike plus the plan to split DVD into 'Qwikster' (reversed in ~3 weeks). Crash 2: Nov 2021 ~$701 (~$70) -> May 2022 ~$163 (~$16), -76%, after the first subscriber loss in a decade. Then password-sharing crackdown + ad tier (ads >50% of signups where offered; ad revenue doubled 2024) -> >300m subs end-2024, stock >$1,000 for most of 2025 (~$110-134 post-split). IPO->2025 peak ~1,000x+; 2012 trough->2025 ~150x+. Rerating split: 2012-21 mostly revenue growth on very high P/E; 2022-25 mostly EPS growth (operating margin ~20% -> ~30%) [margins unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL at each trough: streaming hours and international sub adds kept rising while the stock collapsed; the error was self-inflicted pricing/communication, not demand. Who caught it: Carl Icahn disclosed ~10% in Oct 2012 near the low and made >$1bn [from memory, unverified]. LESSON: when a structurally winning platform crashes on a fixable management error, the drawdown is the opportunity; you must be able to sit through -75% twice.

data.early_signals: engagement/sub growth intact during crashes; errors fixable
data.ended: not ended as of 2025; post-split range
data.eps_vs_rerating: 2022-25 mostly EPS; P/E compressed in 2022 then partially re-expanded
data.lesson: self-inflicted crashes in a winning platform are buyable; survive the drawdown

title: Netflix 2002-2025: two -75% crashes inside a ~1,000x compounder
